explanations.explanation: I get it, friend, because that's exactly how it works with me. If you're not standing right next to my oven, I have NO idea what you're thinking. But David tells the LORD in Psalm 139:2, "You understand my thoughts from afar." Distance doesn't slow the LORD down one bit.

Distance means nothing to the LORD. David puts it to Him plainly in Psalm 139:2: "You understand my thoughts from afar." Close up, far away, it makes no difference to Him. Me, friend, I lose track of my own thoughts from across the bakery.

Every last one of them. The LORD searches out David's path and his lying down, and then comes the big line in Psalm 139:3: "You are aware of all my ways." Walking, resting, everything in between. Friend, I'm aware of maybe three of my ways, and one of them is losing my timer.

Some would already be impressive, friend, I'll give you that. But David goes all the way. Here's his line in Psalm 139:3: "You are aware of all my ways." Not a sample batch, not a handful, the WHOLE tray.

So close it hurts, friend. Most is how I describe my good batches. But the line David gives in Psalm 139:3 is bigger than that: "You are aware of all my ways." The LORD doesn't have a "mostly" setting.

explanations.answer: Before a word is on his tongue
explanations.explanation: Early, early, EARLY. In Psalm 139:4, David prays, "Even before a word is on my tongue, You know all about it, O LORD." The word hasn't even left the station yet and the LORD already knows all about it. Me, friend, I find out what I'm saying about the same time everybody else does.

That's how the rest of us find out, friend. Somebody talks, then we know. But the LORD is way earlier than that. David says in Psalm 139:4, "Even before a word is on my tongue, You know all about it, O LORD."

Friend, the LORD doesn't need a screenshot from the group chat. In Psalm 139:4, David says the LORD knows all about a word even before it's on his tongue. Before it's said, before it's typed, before ANYTHING. I write my cookie recipes down and STILL forget them.

explanations.answer: It's too wonderful for him to reach
explanations.explanation: That's right where David lands. He tells the LORD in Psalm 139:6, "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain." I picture the man just standing there, looking up, speechless. Same, David, same. I've been baking for ages and I still can't explain how my oven knows when to beep.

explanations.answer: It's easy enough for him to explain
explanations.explanation: Not even close, friend. David throws his hands up on this one. Look at Psalm 139:6: "Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain." Too high to reach. Picture me trying to grab the top shelf of the bakery with a mustache that only stretches so far.

explanations.answer: It's something he figured out long ago
explanations.explanation: He hasn't figured it out at ALL, friend, and he says so. In Psalm 139:6, David calls this knowledge "too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain." That's not a man with it all worked out. That's a man looking up and going, WOW.

Sheol sure sounds like a good spot to be left alone, friend. But David says in Psalm 139:8, "If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there." The heavens or Sheol, same answer both times. Wherever David makes his bed, the LORD is there.

No alone time in Sheol either, friend. David covers both ends in Psalm 139:8: "If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there." Two places, and both times, You are there. Believe me, I spent years at the back of a junk drawer, and I STILL got found.

explanations.answer: Guide him and hold him fast
explanations.explanation: Way out by the farthest sea, and the LORD's hand is still right on David. Here's how he says it in Psalm 139:10: "even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast." That's a GRIP. Friend, I can't even hold onto a cookie box when somebody sneezes.

No shove back to the shore here, friend. In Psalm 139:10, David prays, "even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast." Right there, way out by the farthest sea, the LORD guides him and holds on. Nobody gets pushed anywhere.

explanations.answer: Let go and let him wander
explanations.explanation: It's the total opposite, friend. Way out by the farthest sea, David tells the LORD, "Your right hand will hold me fast." That's Psalm 139:10, and that same hand guides him too. Think of me with a fresh tray of cookies. I am NOT letting go.

Not even a little dark, not to the LORD. Look at Psalm 139:12, where David says "even the darkness is not dark to You" and that settles it. The hiding spot he just pictured doesn't hide a thing. Me, friend, I turned off the bakery lights once to sneak a cookie and walked face first into the oven.

I hear you, friend, dark usually means hidden. That's why I do all my secret cookie taste tests with the lights off. But in Psalm 139:12, David says "even the darkness is not dark to You" about the LORD. The darkness David pictured hiding him doesn't hide a thing from Him.

Straight to praise! Thinking about how the LORD knit him together, David says in Psalm 139:14, "I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Out comes worship. Friend, when I look back at my early stamps, praise is NOT the first word that comes out.
Asking why is a very human move, friend. I ask my oven why every single morning. But David goes another way here. He says in Psalm 139:14, "I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made."

Keeping it to himself is not David's style here, friend. He puts it right into Psalm 139:14: "I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." And the whole psalm is for the choirmaster, no less (Psalm 139:1). That's the opposite of keeping quiet.

Made in secret sure sounds hidden, friend, I'll give you that. But David says in Psalm 139:15, "My frame was not hidden from You when I was made in secret, when I was woven together in the depths of the earth." Secret to everybody else, but not to the LORD. Every bit of David's frame was in plain view for Him.

Not hidden at all. In Psalm 139:15, David says his frame "was not hidden from You" even while he was made in secret and woven together in the depths of the earth. Secret, deep down, and STILL in plain view. Meanwhile, friend, I hide one cookie behind the cookie boxes and can't find it myself the next day.

Every one of David's days was on the page before day one. He puts it this way in Psalm 139:16: "all my days were written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be." Not one day had happened yet, and they were already written. Friend, I can't even plan tomorrow's batch until I've hit snooze twice.

After would make the LORD a great record keeper, friend, but David goes way earlier than that. In Psalm 139:16 he says his days were "written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be." Written ahead of time, every one of them. Not a diary, friend, a plan.

Once is close, friend, but David reaches back even further. In Psalm 139:16 he says his days were ordained for him "before one of them came to be." Before day one, they were already in the LORD's book. That's like having the whole cookie box packed before I've stamped a single cookie.

More time sounds like it would do the trick, friend. But in Psalm 139:18, David says that if he tried to count God's thoughts, they would outnumber the grains of sand. That's not a time problem. That's a sand problem. I tried counting the sprinkles in one jar and quit before noon.

No clock in the world fixes this one, friend. Psalm 139:18 is where David says it: "If I were to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand; and when I awake, I am still with You." I lose count of the chocolate chips in ONE batch. He's talking about SAND.

God's enemies, plain and simple. In Psalm 139:20, David says these men "speak of You deceitfully; Your enemies take Your name in vain." They misuse God's own name. It's a heavy turn in the psalm, friend, and David doesn't soften it.

There's no history like that in these verses, friend. The name David gives them in Psalm 139:20 is a lot heavier: "Your enemies take Your name in vain." They speak of God deceitfully. Nothing about a falling out over a borrowed cookie box.

I can see why soldiers came to mind, friend, with all that talk of bloodthirsty men. But David never says where they're from. In Psalm 139:20 he calls them God's enemies, people who "speak of You deceitfully" and who take God's name in vain. What he points to is how they treat God's name.

explanations.answer: He hates them as his enemies
explanations.explanation: David answers his own question with no wiggle room, friend. In Psalm 139:22 he says, "I hate them with perfect hatred; I count them as my enemies." The people who hate the LORD, he counts as his own enemies. Those are strong words, and he says them right to God.

Forgiveness doesn't come up in this line, friend. What David says in Psalm 139:22 is, "I hate them with perfect hatred; I count them as my enemies." The LORD's enemies become David's enemies. He's standing with the LORD against the people who hate Him.

Pity would be gentler, friend, but David doesn't go there. His words in Psalm 139:22 are "I hate them with perfect hatred; I count them as my enemies." Perfect hatred is about as far from pity as it gets.

Yep, David flings the door wide open. In Psalm 139:23 he prays, "Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my concerns." He's inviting the search himself. Friend, I won't even let anybody peek in my oven early, and David is opening up his whole heart.

He really does ask, friend, and that's the twist. In Psalm 139:23 David prays, "Search me, O God, and know my heart" right after all that talk about God's enemies. Most of us would keep the messy parts out of sight, like a baker shoving the burnt batch to the back of the oven before the inspector walks in. David says, come look.

Lead it is, and what a way to close out a psalm. David's last request, in Psalm 139:24, goes like this: "See if there is any offensive way in me; lead me in the way everlasting." First he asks God to look, then he asks God to lead. Not a map, friend. A Guide.

Leave looks a lot like lead, friend, but they go in opposite directions. Back in Psalm 139:7, David asks where he could even flee from God's presence. Then in Psalm 139:24, he doesn't ask God to leave at all. He prays, "lead me in the way everlasting." I know a thing or two about getting left in a drawer, and trust me, lead is the one you want.

Hiding doesn't work in this psalm, friend. Earlier, even the darkness can't hide David from the LORD (Psalm 139:11-12). And the request that closes the psalm, in Psalm 139:24, is "lead me in the way everlasting." Honestly, after years behind the takeout menus, I'd pick being led too.
